newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam promises steps to tackle banking muddle.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam promises steps to tackle banking muddle.

text.p: Vietnam is set to tighten supervision of its chaotic and scandal-ridden banking sector and bring primitive accounting practices closer into line with Western standards, a senior central banker said on Wednesday.

"We are now in transition from a centrally-planned economy to a market system," Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Do Que Luong said. "The banking sector still has the legacy of the old system, so we still have a lot of...problems."
Luong was speaking to reporters after the signing ceremony for a grant from Sweden to finance an independent audit of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of Vietnam (Vietincombank).

Vietincombank, one of four big state-owned commercial banks spun off from the central bank in 1990, will be the second Vietnamese bank to come under the scrutiny of an auditor applying international practices.
Luong said four other banks would be audited early next year.

The financial health of Vietnamese banks has come under increasing scrutiny in recent months and the State Bank has been urged to root out corruption, fraud and incompetence to boost public confidence in the banking system.
A savage editorial in the Communist Party daily Nhan Dan last month said that 4.2 percent of the debt at state-owned commercial banks was overdue.
"Overdue debt" is a catch-all phrase which includes bad or non-performing debt, a Western concept not yet recognised here.
Western analysts, pointing to a weight of politically inspired loans which have sat on bank's balance sheets since the pre-reform years of the early 1980s, say the situation could be a lot worse.
"Until they've got at least two or three years of auditing under their belts, the numbers are still 'guesstimations'," said Bradley Babson, World Bank resident representative in Hanoi.
Luong said the State Bank was working on a classification of bank debt and would issue a circular, based on advice from the International Monetary Fund, later this month.
"We will gradually adopt international standards," he said, but added that the definition of non-performing assets may be less strict than in developed countries.
Luong also said the State Bank would take steps to ensure supervision of the 53 joint stock banks which have sprung up since the government opened banking to the private sector.
These banks, although much smaller than the four main state banks, are said to have higher levels of overdue loans and cannot count on the government to bail them out when trouble looms.

"We at the State Bank of Vietnam will have to take adequate measures to ensure supervision over the joint stock banks," Luong said. "The joint stock banks may...merge to become bigger banks with a larger capital base."
Babson welcomed the State Bank's plans as the first steps towards establishing a legal structure for its supervisory role.

"My feeling here is that the motivation to deepen the reform in the banking sector exists," he said. "The issue is understanding the complexity of the situation and being able to set out a step-by-step approach to moving forward."
